content: Mild sunburn typically presents as red or reddish skin that feels warm to the touch, along with general fatigue and mild dizziness. However, severe sunburn can be life-threatening and is a major risk factor for skin cancer. There is no immediate cure for sunburn; the only remedy is the natural healing process, although certain skin creams can provide symptomatic relief. Sunburn occurs when the amount of UV radiation surpasses the protective capacity of melanin, the pigment in the skin. Individuals with darker skin have higher melanin levels and are less likely to experience sunburn compared to those with lighter skin.g., welding arcs), can also cause similar burns. Additional symptoms may include swelling (edema), itching, peeling skin, rash, nausea, and fever. The affected area may feel warm due to heat emitted from the burn. Sunburns can range in severity from first-degree burns, which cause mild redness and tenderness, to second-degree burns, which may involve blistering. Severe sunburns can be debilitating and may require medical attention. The burn continues to develop over 24 to 72 hours, and peeling skin may occur 3 to 8 days later. Itching and peeling can persist for several weeks. UV radiation is categorized into three subtypes: UVA (380–315 nm), UVB (315–280 nm), and UVC (280–180 nm). The Earth's atmosphere filters out most UVC radiation, but UVA and UVB penetrate in sufficient quantities to cause sunburn. UVB radiation, particularly in the low-frequency range near 320 nm, is most responsible for sunburn due to its high erythemal activity and solar irradiance. UVB radiation damages DNA at the cellular level, which can lead to mutations and an increased risk of skin cancer. Damaged cells release toxins, causing symptoms such as nausea and fever. Extensive cell death can result in peeling skin. The risk of sunburn is higher in tropical regions near the equator (23. However, sunburn can also occur at higher latitudes, especially during late spring and early summer when daylight hours are longer. The intensity of UV radiation depends on the angle of the sun, with the highest risk occurring at noon when shadows are shortest. Certain medications, such as antibiotics, contraceptives, and tranquilizers, can increase sensitivity to UV radiation. Individuals with red hair, freckles, or fair skin are at greater risk of sunburn due to lower melanin levels. To protect the skin, it is recommended to consult the UV index and take appropriate precautions, such as wearing long-sleeved clothing, wide-brimmed hats, and using umbrellas.m. and 3 p.m. is also advised. Broad-spectrum sunscreens that protect against both UVA and UVB are ideal. Waterproof formulations are recommended for water-based activities. Proper application involves using approximately 28 ml (1 oz) of sunscreen to cover the entire body and reapplying after swimming, sweating, or rubbing. Protective clothing, such as welding helmets, should be worn when exposed to artificial UV sources. Eye protection is also essential, as UV radiation can contribute to conditions such as pterygium and cataracts. Wrap-around sunglasses that block UV light are recommended. There is no immediate cure for sunburn, but symptoms can be managed by hydrating the skin with products containing aloe vera or vitamin E. Cool compresses soaked in milk can reduce inflammation and soothe pain due to the lactic acid content. Pain relievers such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen can alleviate discomfort. Blistered skin should be allowed to heal naturally, and antibacterial solutions can prevent infection. Avoid applying lotions or ointments directly to open wounds. The most effective treatment is time, as sunburns typically heal within a few weeks. The most serious long-term consequence of sunburn is an increased risk of skin cancer, particularly malignant melanoma. A single incident of blistering sunburn can double the risk of developing melanoma. Both UVA and UVB radiation are implicated in skin cancer, with UVA penetrating deeper into the skin even in the absence of visible symptoms. Sunburn is not limited to humans; many animals can also suffer from it. Animals with dense fur are generally protected, but those with sparse or hairless skin, such as pigs and hippopotamuses, are more vulnerable. Variations in pigmentation, fur density, and genetic factors, such as albinism, can influence susceptibility. Plants can also experience sunburn, with damage to tissue caused by excessive sunlight. In trees, sunburn (or sunscald) typically affects bark tissue and can lead to long-term damage. Sunburn is closely related to other conditions such as hyperthermia (heat stroke) and windburn.
